description: We are To Mars and Back: five TUM students and one from HHN, studying computer science, data science and management. We bring skills in coding (TypeScript, React, Python), 3D maps, computer vision, data science and project management. Our project Mars Seek plans a safe route for the first human walk on Mars and guides the astronaut with a helmet that spots dangers on its own. We believe space tools should be simple to use in a spacesuit and work without help from Earth.
summary:
Mars Seek is a survival guide for the first human walk on Mars. In the habitat, the crew picks science stops in Jezero crater, and Mars Seek plans the safest route a suited astronaut can walk. The route avoids slopes over 20°, fits one 8-hour excursion and always stays close enough to walk back. Outside, the astronaut follows the same route in a 3D helmet view built from real terrain. The helmet’s computer vision spots rocks, loose sand and drop-offs and re-plans the route. It also detects a dust storm from the camera alone and guides the astronaut back to the habitat.

The challenge asks for a hyperlocal map that layers several NASA datasets for one Marswalk. We combined HiRISE, CTX, THEMIS, CRISM, a 1 m elevation model, and Perseverance photos and weather into one route the crew can actually walk.

This matters because a message from Mars can take up to 22 minutes to reach Earth. The first astronauts will have to decide alone, and Mars Seek gives them the information to decide safely.

details:
Mars Seek: Help Is 22 Minutes Away

A message from Mars can take up to 22 minutes to reach Earth. When the first astronauts step outside on Mars, there will be no one to ask in time. A steep slope, a field of boulders, a dust storm rolling in: the crew will have to decide on their own. Mars Seek gives them the map and the eyes to decide safely.
What is Mars Seek?

Mars Seek is a survival guide for one walk on Mars. Our site is Jezero crater, where the Perseverance rover is exploring right now. Our science goal: search for signs of ancient life. The crew collects the samples Perseverance left on the surface and reaches Cheyava Falls, the rock that may hold the rover’s strongest clue.

One route, three moments: Plan it in the habitat. Walk it with a tablet and a helmet. React when Mars surprises you.

1. Plan: The Safest Route in One Click

The crew picks the science stops, and Mars Seek finds the safest round trip a suited astronaut can walk.

  • No slopes steeper than 20° on foot (15° by crew rover), worked out from a 1-metre NASA elevation model.
  • One 8-hour excursion: if the plan does not fit, Mars Seek says so.
  • Always close enough to walk back: lines on the map show how far the crew can go and still return home in time.
  • Radiation dose, weather and the best time to leave, from real Curiosity and Perseverance measurements.
  • A real rover photo for every stop, so the crew knows what it will look like before they get there.

2. Walk: A Tablet That Talks, a Helmet That Sees

On the walk, the tablet gives turn-by-turn directions with voice, shows the way back to base and the conditions outside. It installs like an app and works offline, because there is no internet on Mars.

Through the helmet, the astronaut sees a 3D Mars built from real NASA terrain data. Orbit cannot see small rocks, but the helmet can. Two helmet cameras measure depth and find rocks, steep ground, loose sand and drop-offs from the pixels alone. Every rock is outlined on the visor, a hazard map fills in as the astronaut walks, and if the way is blocked, the route is re-planned on the spot. We also ran the same detector on a real Perseverance stereo photo.


3. React: The Helmet Sees the Storm Itself

Dust storms on Mars can grow until they cover the whole planet. In a storm, waiting 22 minutes for advice from Earth is not an option.

So the helmet camera watches the air, about once a second, right on the suit, with no link to Earth. Two checks must agree: fast pixel measurements (lost detail in the distance, haze, contrast) and CLIP, a small AI model running in the browser. When both say “dust storm”, the helmet stops the walk, raises an alert and guides the astronaut back to the habitat.

The storm in the helmet demo is simulated, but we tested the detector on real NASA images: Curiosity’s view of the June 2018 global dust storm reads “dust storm, 84% visibility lost”.

Built on NASA Data

Every layer comes from NASA missions: HiRISE and CTX images from orbit, the 1 m HiRISE elevation model (USGS), THEMIS heat maps, CRISM mineral maps, and Perseverance’s route, Navcam photos and MEDA weather. We are honest about what is simulated: small rocks, the sky, the suit’s numbers, the astronaut’s position and the dust storm in the helmet demo.

How We Built It

TypeScript, React, Leaflet for maps, three.js for the 3D helmet and Python to prepare the NASA data. CLIP runs in the browser through Transformers.js. The site is hosted on Vercel, and Claude helped us write the code. Everything runs in a web browser: no installs, no special hardware.

Our Mission

The next giant leap will not be about getting to Mars. It will be about coming back from every walk. Mars Seek was born from one idea: astronauts far from Earth need tools that are simple enough to use in a spacesuit and smart enough to work on their own.

Plan safe. Walk safe. Come back.

Github link: https://github.com/danyarwx/martian-map
